title: Harvard Is Punishing Postdocs for Succeeding
text:
Harvard Is Punishing Postdocs for Succeeding | The Harvard Crimson 
 The Harvard Crimson News Metro Opinion Arts Blog Magazine Multimedia Sports Newsletter Print Delivery Tips Donate Programs Advertisement Advertisement Opinion Harvard Is Punishing Postdocs for Succeeding
 By Megan L. Blonigen By Hannah A. Grunwald , Contributing Opinion Writer Hannah A. Grunwald is a postdoctoral researcher in the Genetics Department at Harvard Medical School. In the summer of 2021, I won a prestigious research fellowship from the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation to fund my research in cryptic genetics. I didn’t know then that because of Harvard’s stipendee policy, I’d inadvertently put myself in financial jeopardy.
 On November 10, the Harvard Academic Workers-United Auto Workers, which represents lecturers, preceptors, and postdoctoral fellows, like myself, went on strike to protest Harvard’s insufficient progress on key contract proposals. Most of our sticking points are the ones you’d expect: fair compensation, access to childcare and other family benefits that are already available to tenure-track faculty, and union security — the rights to file grievances and collect union dues.
 But we have one final issue on which the Harvard administration has refused to bargain with us. Harvard is attempting to exclude hundreds of postdocs from the union for the crime of having been awarded fellowships.
 By winning a fellowship, I started my postdoctoral position in an odd classification: what Harvard calls a “stipendee.” Harvard’s human resources office distinguishes “employee” from “stipendee” postdocs; the latter are defined as researchers “who may work under the direction of a Harvard faculty mentor, but to whom payment is in the form of a stipend.” Stipendees “are not considered to be employees and therefore are ineligible for certain benefits,” the office adds.
 Although the only distinction seems to be in the source of funding, Harvard treats stipendees and employees very differently.
 From the outside, it’s impossible to identify the difference between researchers who are stipendees and employees. We do the same job, attend the same meetings, use the same Harvard-provided equipment, and follow the same policies. For some of us, our paychecks still come through Harvard. Our intellectual property belongs to Harvard. Perhaps the only difference is that, generally, employees receive W2 tax forms, while stipendees do not. On the inside, living as a stipendee can mean thousands of dollars less in take-home pay.
 In 2024, I wrote and won a National Institutes of Health grant for an expansion of the same project. Overnight, I became an employee. Aside from my financial situation, nothing about my employment has changed. I do identical work. I run the same experiments. I have the same obligations. My publications are tied to Harvard. This is as true now as it was when I was a Damon Runyon fellow. The fundamental difference? Harvard officially recognizes that I work for them.
 As a stipendee, I was barred from choosing a subset of the health plans. For tax purposes, I was also considered a self-employed contractor and required to pay extra quarterly taxes. Harvard considers the contributions to stipendee health plans as taxable income, effectively maintaining the ruse that these employees somehow do not work for Harvard. As a reward for winning a highly esteemed fellowship and saving Harvard from paying my salary, I made considerably less than my colleagues doing identical work.
 Now, in addition to presenting financial barriers, Harvard is refusing to allow stipendees to be counted as members of HAW-UAW, despite the fact that stipendees voted with other postdocs to form our union. By excluding stipendees from HAW, workers who already lose money — despite helping their labs cover their salary — would further lose access to anything we end up gaining in our contract, even in the face of the patently obvious reality that stipendees and employees work for Harvard in precisely the same capacity.
 This betrayal is bad enough by itself, but when compared to other peer institutions, it’s shocking. At institutions like the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and Weill Cornell Medicine, employees who win major fellowships and have their salaries paid by outside sources are still considered employees and included in academic unions. In fact, the National Labor Relations Board recently ruled that at the University of Pennsylvania, workers who would be considered stipendees at Harvard must be included in their postdoc union.
 The exclusion of these workers from our union is fundamentally bad labor practice. It puts postdocs at risk by denying access to baseline protections codified in a union contract, and it eliminates channels for recourse in response to dangerous work situations. Furthermore, by carving out stipendees from HAW, Harvard is doing wide-ranging damage to academic workers. Setting a precedent that lets universities punish their employees for winning fellowships weakens academic worker unions all across America.
 Beyond that, it is an illogical and inefficient policy. The constant onboarding and offboarding of employees who were stipendees is inherently an administrative burden that the University can ill afford. The discrepancy in pay and benefits is enough to scare off the most ambitious researcher from applying for external funding. At a time when federal funding is increasingly fraught, and department budgets are being tightened under Harvard’s austerity measures, labs need their researchers’ salaries covered. Thus, the University cannot afford to be disincentivizing fellowship applications.
 It’s shameful that Harvard would treat any of its workers with such blatant disdain. It’s shameful that Harvard punishes, rather than celebrates, the achievements of some of its brightest and most creative scholars.
 “Stipendees” are, in every measure but name, Harvard’s academic workers. They should be part of Harvard’s academic workers’ union.
 Hannah A. Grunwald is a postdoctoral researcher in the Genetics Department at Harvard Medical School.
